source_refs.note: Topic 9.15 with Figs. 9.24 to 9.26, Example 9.9 and the Do You Know box (PDF 213-215, printed 210-212).

blocks.text: A source of electrical energy, say a cell or a battery, when connected across a resistance maintains a steady current through it (Fig. 9.24). The cell continuously supplies energy, which is dissipated in the resistance of the circuit. Suppose that when a steady current has been established, a charge Q passes through any cross-section of the circuit in time t. During its motion this charge enters the cell at its low-potential end and leaves at its high-potential end; the source must supply energy W to the positive charge to compel it to go to the point of high potential.

blocks.alt: A cell of emf E connected to a resistance R drives a steady current I round the circuit. A note says the cell uses chemical energy to move charge from its negative to its positive terminal, and this energy per coulomb is the emf.
blocks.caption: A cell maintaining a current through a resistance R (original diagram after Figure 9.24).

blocks.title: Electromotive force
blocks.text: The emf E of a source is the energy supplied to unit charge by the cell: E = W/Q ... (9.41).

Electromotive force is not a force, and we do not measure it in newtons. The unit of emf is the joule/coulomb, which is the volt (V). The energy supplied by the cell to the charge carriers is derived from the conversion of chemical energy into electrical energy inside the cell.

Like other components in a circuit, a cell also offers some resistance. This resistance is due to the electrolyte present between the two electrodes of the cell and is called the internal resistance of the cell. Thus a cell of emf E having an internal resistance r is equivalent to a source of pure emf E with a resistance r in series (Fig. 9.25).

blocks.alt: Inside a dashed outline marked the cell, an emf E is drawn in series with a small resistance r, the internal resistance, between the two terminals. The caption gives the terminal voltage V = E - I r, less than E when a current flows.
blocks.caption: A cell as an emf E with internal resistance r (original diagram after Figure 9.25).

blocks.text: Consider a cell of emf E and internal resistance r (Fig. 9.26). A voltmeter of infinite resistance measures the potential difference across the external resistance R, which is the potential difference V across the terminals of the cell. The current through the circuit is I = E/(R + r), or E = IR + Ir ... (9.42). Here IR = V is the terminal potential difference of the cell in the presence of current I. When the switch S is open, no current passes through the resistance, and the voltmeter reads the emf E as the terminal voltage. Thus the terminal voltage in the presence of current (switch on) is less than the emf E by Ir. A voltmeter connected across the terminals of a cell measures (a) the emf of the cell on open circuit and (b) the terminal potential difference on a closed circuit (Do You Know).

blocks.alt: A cell of emf E and internal resistance r with a high-resistance voltmeter across its terminals. A rheostat R and a switch S complete the outer circuit. A box says that with S open the voltmeter reads E, and with S closed it reads E - I r.
blocks.caption: Measuring terminal potential difference with a voltmeter and switch (original diagram after Figure 9.26).

blocks.text: Interpreting Eq. 9.42 by energy: the left side, the emf E, is the energy gained by unit charge as it passes through the cell from its negative to its positive terminal. The right side accounts for the use of this energy as the current passes round the circuit: as unit charge passes through, a part of the energy equal to Ir is dissipated in the cell, and the rest, given by the potential drop IR, is dissipated in the external resistance R. Thus the emf gives the energy supplied to unit charge by the cell, and the potential drops across the various elements account for the dissipation of this energy into other forms as the unit charge passes through them. The emf is the cause and the potential difference is its effect: the emf is always present even when no current is drawn through the cell, but the potential difference across a conductor is zero when no current flows through it.

blocks.title: Example 9.9
blocks.text: The potential difference between the terminals of a battery on open circuit is 2.2 V. When it is connected across a resistance of 5.0 ohm, the potential falls to 1.8 V. Calculate the current and the internal resistance of the battery. Solution: E = 2.2 V, R = 5.0 ohm, V = 1.8 V. I = V/R = 1.8 V/5.0 ohm = 0.36 A. E = V + Ir: 2.2 V = 1.8 V + 0.36 A x r, so r = 1.1 V A^-1 = 1.1 ohm.

blocks.caption: Emf and terminal potential difference
rows: energy given to unit charge by the source
energy used by unit charge in the external circuit
V = E - Ir, less than E

blocks.prompt: Why does the terminal potential difference of a battery decrease when the current drawn from it is increased (constructed response 9.6)? A 12 V battery with internal resistance 0.2 ohm is connected to a 3.6 ohm resistor; find the terminal voltage (numerical 9.10).
blocks.explanation: V = E - Ir: the drop Ir across the internal resistance grows with the current, so less of the emf is left across the terminals. I = E/(R + r) = 12/3.8 = 3.16 A, and V = IR = 3.16 x 3.6 = 11.4 V.

items: Emf E = W/Q (9.41): energy per unit charge given by the source, in volts; from chemical energy in a cell. Internal resistance r of the electrolyte: I = E/(R + r), E = IR + Ir (9.42); terminal voltage V = E - Ir; open circuit V = E.
Emf is the cause, potential difference the effect. Example 9.9: I = 0.36 A, r = 1.1 ohm.
